Isolation Precautions

precaution by route · when isolation ends · protective precautions in neutropeniaWhich way does it travel, and whom does the precaution shield?

Source vignette Pt – febrile, lethargic, hypotensive infant moving to intensive care on antibiotics · Labs – gram-negative diplococci on the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Gram stain · Q – which precaution to start; choices were airborne, contact, droplet, neutropenic and standard
Bottom line
  • Match the precaution to how the organism travels: droplets of 5 microns or more drop within 3 to 6 feet and need a surgical mask; airborne particles under 5 microns hang in room air and need an N95 respirator in a negative-pressure room; contact organisms ride on hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves.
  • Standard precautions already cover every patient, so they are never the added answer; neutropenic precautions reverse the direction and shield the patient from everyone else.
  • Isolation ends by organism: 24 hours of effective antibiotics for meningococcus and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), 5 days of antibiotics for pertussis, every lesion crusted for varicella, and clinical improvement, usually with 3 negative sputum smears, for tuberculosis (TB).

Two questions sort every case: what size the particle is, and whose safety the precaution serves. A large droplet falls within 3 to 6 feet of the patient; a droplet nucleus can stay suspended in indoor air for several hours; a contact organism moves on hands, skin, stool and shared objects.

Precaution by route
PrecautionOrganismsGear and room
StandardEvery patientHand hygiene for all; add gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when blood or body fluid exposure is expected Hand hygiene is the single most important step against hospital-acquired spread.
DropletMeningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis), Hib, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, pertussis, adenovirus, mumps, rubella Adenovirus also spreads on fingers and shared objects, so adenovirus pneumonia adds contact precautions to droplet.Surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; private room
AirborneTuberculosis, measles, SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) SARS adds droplet and contact precautions to airborne.Fitted N95 respirator; single negative-pressure room; staff without immunity kept out of a measles room
Airborne plus contactVaricella; disseminated zosterN95 and a negative-pressure room, plus gown and gloves
ContactRSV (respiratory syncytial virus), C. difficile, scabies, E. coli O157:H7 in a diapered or incontinent patient, MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers It comes from a preformed toxin and does not pass from person to person, so it needs no contact precautions.Gown and gloves, ideally a private room; dedicated equipment; soap-and-water hand washing for C. difficile Alcohol-based hand rubs do not kill C. difficile spores.
Protective (reverse)Severe neutropenia, ANC (absolute neutrophil count) under 500, as after chemotherapy or stem cell transplantHand hygiene and a private, filtered-air room; bar fresh flowers, plants and animals; bar rectal thermometers, enemas and suppositories
When isolation ends
OrganismEnds when
Meningococcus24 hours of effective antibiotics
Hib24 hours of effective antibiotics
Pertussis5 days after antibiotics start Without antibiotics, isolation lasts 3 weeks. In practice: a patient treated at home is isolated for at least 4 weeks from onset and until symptoms subside.
MumpsGland swelling subsides
TuberculosisClinical improvement plus 3 negative sputum AFB (acid-fast bacilli) smears in a row Release usually requires 3 negative smears over 2 days, at least 1 from early morning.
Measles4 days after rash onset An immunocompromised patient may shed virus for longer, so isolation lasts the whole illness. A mild rash and fever 1 to 3 weeks after the MMR vaccine come from the vaccine strain: no respiratory isolation, but keep the child away from immunocompromised people.
Varicella and disseminated zosterEvery lesion crusted
Scabies24 hours after effective therapy starts
C. difficile and RSVDuration of illness
Protective (reverse)Neutrophil count recovers

Isolate on suspicion: a child with suspected measles, or a patient under evaluation for TB, goes into airborne isolation before the results return. Close contacts of meningococcal disease also need chemoprophylaxis (see ).

Pause point
Infant in shock; CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci Offered as airborne precautions or contact precautions What size of particle carries meningococcus? → Large droplets: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics
Fever and a faint rash 10 days after the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine Offered as airborne precautions, as for measles Wild virus, or the vaccine strain? → Vaccine-strain rash: no respiratory isolation; keep the child away from immunocompromised people
Leukemia in induction chemotherapy, ANC 200, temperature check due Offered as a rectal thermometer or contact precautions Who is being protected from whom? → The patient: neutropenic precautions, so no rectal thermometer

Every patient already gets standard precautions; the question asks what to add on top.

Practice
  1. 3 yo F with 12 hours of fever, lethargy and a spreading petechial rash; BP 68/36; CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci; intravenous antibiotics are running, and she is moving to the pediatric ICU (intensive care unit) → Droplet precautions → Neisseria meningitidis: surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet until 24 hours of effective antibiotics
  2. 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration → Airborne precautions → measles: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
  3. 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus → Contact precautions → RSV spreads mainly by hands and contaminated surfaces: gown and gloves
  4. 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago → Three negative sputum AFB smears → active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation ends when the patient is improving clinically on effective therapy and three consecutive sputum smears are negative
  5. 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 → Airborne and contact precautions → varicella: N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves until every lesion has crusted
  6. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions → Rectal temperature measurement → neutropenic precautions protect the patient: no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositories, no fresh flowers or plants
  7. 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR (polymerase chain reaction) positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration → Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing → alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores

Scabies covers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household.
Infectious Diarrhea covers the workup and treatment of C. difficile and E. coli O157:H7.
Transferable rule

Size the particle, then name who is protected. Droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet need a surgical mask; particles that hang in room air need an N95 and a negative-pressure room; organisms on skin, stool or surfaces need a gown and gloves; neutropenic precautions protect the patient.

Unchecked attributeAirborne precautions: the right idea, a respiratory route, with the wrong particle size; meningococcus travels in large droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet, and airborne isolation is for TB, measles and varicella.
Salient decoyContact precautions: a septic, possibly petechial infant in the ICU feels like a gown-and-gloves patient, but meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets, not by skin or surfaces.
True-fact-wrong-slotStandard precautions: they apply to every patient, including this one, but they are the baseline, not the transmission-based precaution the organism requires.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenic precautions: the direction is reversed; they protect an immunocompromised patient, and this infant is the source of infection.
